Moses Stuart
mō'zəz stoo'ərt
n. (Moses Stuart, 1780–1852, Andover professor of sacred literature, father of American biblical philology)
Hebrew Mosheh, drawn out; Scottish surname Stuart, a steward.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Moses Stuart taught sacred literature at Andover for thirty-eight years and did more than any other American of his generation to put Hebrew and Greek study on a scholarly footing in this country. He wrote the first serviceable American Hebrew grammar, set up a press that could print Hebrew and Arabic type, translated German grammatical and lexical works, and trained the men who became the first generation of American orientalists, Edward Robinson among them. He wrote commentaries on Hebrews, Romans, Revelation, and Daniel, and he answered Channing on the Trinity and the deity of Christ in a public exchange that established him nationally. He also introduced the tools of German criticism to American seminaries, and used them himself to argue for a shortened canon of the Old Testament apocryphal borderlands and for readings his own colleagues judged unsafe. 2Ti 2:15 is the standard his students inherited, “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines philology as the study of language and its etymology, and grammar as the art of speaking or writing a language with propriety.

expand to see more

PHILOL'OGY, n. Primarily, a love of words, or a desire to know the origin and construction of language; criticism; grammatical learning.

GRAM'MAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety or correctness, according to established usage.

CRIT'ICISM, n. The art of judging with propriety concerning any object; the examination of literary works.

Modern Corruption

He gave America the tools of biblical scholarship, and the tools arrived with their German assumptions attached.

expand to see more

Stuart's achievement is real and the dictionary does not diminish it. A church that cannot read its own Scriptures in the original languages is at the mercy of whoever can, and Stuart ended that dependence for American Protestantism. His exchange with Channing is a model of exegetical polemic, and his insistence that a text means what its grammar and usage allow is the right instinct, the same instinct Isa 8:20 commands.

The corruption to name is the freight. Stuart imported Gesenius and the German grammarians, and with them came the governing premise of that scholarship, that the biblical books are to be read as the ordinary products of their period, with predictive prophecy and Mosaic authorship open to revision on internal grounds. Stuart himself resisted much of this, but his successors at Andover did not, and the documentary hypothesis and the division of Isaiah entered American seminaries through doors he had built. 2Pe 1:21 is the premise the dictionary holds against the whole method: the prophecy came not by the will of man, but “holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek orthotomeo (G3718), to cut straight; phero (G5342), to bear, be moved; Hebrew torah (H8451), law.

Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, rightly divide; 2 Timothy 2:15.

Greek spoudazo (G4704) — to be diligent, study; 2 Timothy 2:15.

Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction; Isaiah 8:20.

Greek diermeneuo (G1329) — to expound; Luke 24:27.

Greek phero (G5342) — to bear, carry, be moved; 2 Peter 1:21.

Usage

"“rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) — what he trained men to do."

"“holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21) — the premise the method lost."

"“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — his own best instinct."
